title: Fish Species Diversity, Seasonal Dynamics and Land Use Land Cover Associations With Fish Assemblages in the Gulf of Lake Tana, Ethiopia
content:
ABSTRACT

Lake Tana, Ethiopia, harbours the world's only remaining cyprinid species flock, making it globally significant for conservation. Yet, these resources face mounting anthropogenic pressures from overfishing and land use changes. We assessed fish assemblage structure and seasonal dynamics in the Gulf of Lake Tana from September 2024 to August 2025 and land use land cover (LULC) changes from 2000 to 2025 using Landsat and Sentinel imagery. Fish specimens were sampled monthly from fishers at landing sites employing gillnets of varying mesh sizes. The specimens were identified to species level and analysed using Shannon diversity (H′), evenness (J), dominance (C) and Index of Relative Importance (%IRI). Exploratory multivariate analyses (non-metric multidimensional scaling [NMDS] and principal component analysis [PCA] of four seasonal aggregates) were used to describe seasonal assemblage patterns. A total of 2764 specimens representing 18 species were recorded, dominated by endemic Labeobarbus spp. (81.8%), followed by Oreochromis niloticus (11.9%) and Clarias gariepinus (6.3%). Diversity was moderate (H′ = 2.60) and differed significantly among four hydrological seasons (individual-based permutation test, 9999 permutations: p = 0.0024), being highest in the dry season (H′ = 2.596). After Bonferroni correction, dry-season H′ differed significantly from pre-rainy (Hutcheson t-test, t = 3.84, adjusted p = 0.0006) and post-rainy H′ (p = 0.036), but not from rainy-season H′ (adjusted p = 0.066). Evenness was high in all seasons (J = 0.87–0.95). Sex ratios were female-biased in the catches of 12 of 18 species (χ 2, p < 0.001). Between 2000 and 2025, cropland and settlements expanded to nearly 60% of the mapped area, whereas wetlands declined by 92.7%. Because, fish data cover a single year and no environmental covariates were measured, these LULC trends are presented only as landscape context that is associated with the current assemblage composition. The findings provide baseline data for further studies, testing these associations directly, and support the need for watershed rehabilitation, buffer zone protection and sustained fisheries monitoring to protect the lake's globally unique cyprinid flock.
